standard_prerequisites.name: Cardinal
standard_prerequisites.statement: A cardinal is an ordinal that is not equinumerous with any of its elements.
standard_prerequisites.use: The proof puts alpha in a member b of X that is a cardinal and uses that fact to get alpha is smaller than b (source lines 697-699), and the conclusion is exactly that union X is not equinumerous with any of its elements (source lines 701-702).

standard_prerequisites.name: Cardinal comparison
standard_prerequisites.statement: For ordinals alpha and b, alpha is less than b as a cardinal when alpha is equinumerous with a member of b; the relation is transitive and behaves monotonically under subsets.
standard_prerequisites.use: The chain alpha < b <= union X, hence alpha != union X, is the core of the proof (source lines 698-701).

core_obligations: Observe that the union of X is an ordinal, so that cardinal comparison can be applied to its members (source line 696).

For an ordinal alpha in the union of X, find a cardinal b in X with alpha in b, use that b is a cardinal to conclude alpha is strictly smaller than b, and use b subseteq union X to conclude b is at most union X (source lines 696-700).
Chain the comparisons to get that alpha is not equinumerous with union X and generalise over all ordinals in union X, which is the definition of a cardinal (source lines 700-702).

proof_roadmap.step: Note that union X is an ordinal and pick beta in the union, witnessed by a cardinal b in X.
Use that b is a cardinal to get beta < b, and b subseteq union X to get b <= union X.
Conclude beta != union X and generalise, so union X is a cardinal.

difficulty_reason: The counted unit is the author's own proposition unioncardinalscardinal at source lines 691-693: if every member of X is a cardinal, then the union of X is a cardinal. The proof at source lines 695-703 does not follow from the definition of a cardinal by a single unfolding. It first has to be seen that the union of X is an ordinal, which is left to the reader as an easy check because unions of ordinals are ordinals, and the real content is the second half: given an ordinal alpha in the union of X, one must find a cardinal b in X with alpha in b, use that b is a cardinal to conclude alpha is strictly smaller than b as a cardinal, then use b subseteq union X to obtain that b is at most union X, and chain the two strict/smaller comparisons to conclude alpha is not equinumerous with union X. The proof uses three distinct closure facts (union of ordinals, subset of a union, transitivity of the cardinal comparison) and the generalisation step at the end is what converts the pointwise statement into the cardinality assertion. No result outside the retained text is used.
